summary: Year 3 learners classify lines by orientation and relationship, not by their look: horizontal (flat like the horizon or a tabletop), vertical (upright like a wall or standing person), parallel (always the same distance apart, never meeting however far extended) and perpendicular (meeting or crossing at a right angle). The core work is replacing appearance-based judgements (that parallel must be equal length, or that only horizontal/vertical pairs count) and separating the two relationship words. The practical test for parallel is extending the lines and checking that the gap between them stays the same; a drawing can only be extended so far, so 'not meeting on the page' supports, but does not by itself prove, 'never meeting'. The practical test for perpendicular is checking the angle where the lines meet against a known right angle, in any orientation.
misconceptions: Thinks parallel lines must be the same length
Thinks lines only count as parallel/perpendicular when they are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs

activities.title: Extend and rotate: what parallel really means
steps: Start with two lines on screen or drawn on paper that look 'wonky' and are different lengths; predict aloud whether they will ever cross if extended, and say why before testing.

Extend both lines all the way to the edges (press an EXTEND button, or continue the lines with a ruler across a large sheet), observe whether they meet, and measure the gap between them at several places to see whether it stays the same.

Drag or draw a second pair that looks nearly parallel but leans enough to converge within the page or screen; extend them and watch them cross. Note that a very tiny lean might only cross beyond the edge, and the narrowing gap still shows the lines are not parallel.
Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal and confirm the relationship is kept when tilted.

Use a right-angle checker (the corner of a card, a set-square, or a detector that glows green) on a perpendicular crossing pair tilted to 45 degrees to confirm a right angle is still a right angle whichever way the corner faces.
Label real photos or scenes — railway tracks, ladder rungs, window frames, the letter H — as parallel or perpendicular, including tilted and unequal examples.
activities.insight: Parallel means staying the same distance apart and never meeting however far extended — not being flat and not being equal in length; and a right angle stays a right angle at any orientation.

activities.title: Anchor and separate the four words
steps: Point to a horizontal line in the room and a vertical one, naming each and saying a memory hook (horizontal = flat like the horizon; vertical = upright like a wall).
For each pair of lines shown, point and say which relationship it is: 'these run alongside and never meet = parallel'; 'these make a right angle = perpendicular'.
Mark up letters and shapes: find the parallel verticals and the perpendicular cross-bar in an H; mark a rectangle's parallel sides and perpendicular corners.
Deliberately practise cases that are easy to mix up — a right-angle crossing (perpendicular, not parallel) and a vertical line asked for when a horizontal one is shown.
activities.insight: The four terms name distinct ideas: horizontal/vertical are orientations, parallel/perpendicular are relationships between two lines; naming while pointing keeps them apart.

activities.title: Predict, observe, explain and a sorting check
steps: Given two genuinely parallel lines drawn tilted and of different lengths, predict whether they will ever cross if extended across the room, and give a reason before extending.
Extend them and compare the result to the prediction; explain any surprise.
Sort a set of line-pairs into parallel / perpendicular / neither, including tilted parallel pairs and rotated right-angle crosses chosen so appearance-based answers fail.
Match each word (horizontal, vertical, parallel, perpendicular) to a picture, including non-standard orientations.
activities.insight: A correct answer must rest on the relationship (same distance / never meet; meet at a right angle), not on tilt or length; the reason a learner gives before testing reveals which rule they are using.

checkQuestion: Show the child two lines that are genuinely parallel but drawn TILTED (diagonal) and of clearly DIFFERENT lengths. Ask: 'Are these two lines parallel?' Then, whatever they say: 'How do you know?'
checkAnswer: Yes — they are parallel. They stay exactly the same distance apart all the way along and would never meet, however far you extended them. Their tilt and their different lengths don't matter; parallel is about staying the same distance apart and never meeting.
